analysis.one_liner: Phases out routine antibiotics in livestock feed unless makers prove they don't breed drug-resistant infections.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Kennedy with the support of 3 senators, the bill was referred to the Senate health committee on May 13, 2002 and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the routine, non-medical feeding of human-use antibiotics to livestock and poultry unless the drug's maker could show no risk to human health from resistant bacteria. Drugs in the same chemical class as critical human antibiotics — including cipro-type fluoroquinolones used in poultry — would have been pulled from feed and water use within two years unless proven safe. To ease the transition, it authorized payments to farmers who cut back, with priority for family farms.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who rely on antibiotics still working when they get sick. The bill's findings cite the National Academy of Sciences linking antibiotics in food animals to resistant bacteria and human disease, and the FDA's conclusion that poultry use of fluoroquinolones is a significant cause of resistant human infections. It also helps farmers who want to cut antibiotic use, with transition payments prioritized for family farms.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes animal feed containing fluoroquinolones (the cipro class) legally unsafe unless the drug's sponsor shows reasonable certainty of no harm to human health from antimicrobial resistance, effectively ending their routine use in poultry.

It requires the withdrawal of approvals for 'critical antimicrobial drugs' — penicillins, tetracyclines, macrolides, and other drugs used in humans — for nontherapeutic animal use within 2 years, unless the sponsor demonstrates no harm from resistance.
It authorizes Agriculture Department payments to livestock and poultry producers who substantially reduce nontherapeutic antibiotic use, with priority for family-owned and family-operated farms.

The bill's findings cite the National Academy of Sciences' conclusion that there is a link between antibiotic use in food animals, bacterial resistance, and human disease, and the FDA's 2000 conclusion that fluoroquinolone use in poultry is a significant cause of resistant human infections.

analysis.who_pays: Livestock and poultry producers who rely on routine antibiotics for growth promotion and disease prevention would bear transition costs, and animal-drug makers would lose a large feed-additive market. The National Academy of Sciences estimated the cost to the average consumer at no more than $5 to $10 per year, and the transition payments would be funded by taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Producers would face the cost of switching from routine antibiotics to other disease-management practices during a two-year phase-out; the National Academy of Sciences estimated consumers would pay no more than $5 to $10 per year, but farm-level transition costs would fall hardest on producers using the drugs most heavily.

The bill shifts the burden of proof to drug sponsors, who would have to demonstrate a reasonable certainty of no harm from resistance or lose their animal-feed approvals within two years — a standard the animal-drug industry considered difficult to meet.
The farmer assistance section is an open-ended appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary'), so its cost to taxpayers is unspecified.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit — keeping first-line antibiotics effective for treating sick people — is large and, per the National Academy of Sciences estimate cited in the bill, would cost consumers at most $5-10 a year. The real costs fall on a narrow set of concentrated interests: producers using routine antibiotics and the makers of feed-additive drugs, which is precisely why the bill faced industry resistance. The design eases the transition with payments and preserves treatment of genuinely sick animals under veterinary care.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2002 and sent to the Senate health committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the Preservation of Antibiotics for Human Treatment Act on May 13, 2002, joined by Sens. Jack Reed and Jeff Bingaman — three senators in all.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never held a hearing, reported the bill, or brought it to a vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Producers that use routine antibiotics to speed growth in livestock and poultry, and the animal-drug companies that sell them feed additives, kept their market and practices intact for the rest of the Congress. The public got no protection from antibiotic resistance from this bill.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its findings on the public-health risks of routine antibiotic use in livestock.

for.name: Sens. Jack Reed and Jeff Bingaman
for.role: U.S. Senators from Rhode Island and New Mexico
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsors.

for.name: American Medical Association and allied medical and public-health organizations
for.what_they_did: Had adopted resolutions opposing nontherapeutic antimicrobial use in animal agriculture, positions the bill's findings cite in support.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral; never reported the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or floor report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Animal-drug manufacturers and livestock industry groups
against.role: Producers and sellers of feed-additive antibiotics
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on nontherapeutic antibiotic use; the bill's own findings note that one fluoroquinolone manufacturer was already contesting FDA's proposed withdrawal of poultry uses in court proceedings that can drag on for years.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred. All three supporters — the sponsor and both cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on, but the chamber as a whole never weighed in.

industries.industry: Animal-drug manufacturers (veterinary arms of pharmaceutical companies)
industries.note: The bill forces sponsors to prove a drug's animal-feed use poses no resistance risk to human health or lose approval within two years, covering penicillins, tetracyclines, macrolides, fluoroquinolones and other human-use classes. The bill's findings note FDA already moved to withdraw poultry fluoroquinolones and that one manufacturer was contesting that withdrawal, with past withdrawal proceedings lasting 6 to 20 years — the bill was designed to cut through that delay.

industries.industry: Livestock and poultry producers using routine antibiotics (industrial operations)
industries.note: Growth promotion, feed efficiency, and routine disease-prevention uses of critical antibiotics would be phased out in two years, forcing changes in how large operations raise animals. Their continued routine use of these drugs is what the scientific findings link to resistant infections in people.
Transition payments for reducing nontherapeutic antibiotic use would be prioritized for family-owned and family-operated farms, easing their costs relative to larger competitors.
